title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays

understand.question: Given two already-sorted integer arrays, what would the middle value (median) be if they were combined into one sorted list, without actually building that giant list in slow time?
understand.plainExplanation: Imagine two sorted stacks of test scores. If you poured them into one combined sorted pile, the median splits the pile into two equal-sized halves: every score in the left half is <= every score in the right half.
understand.inputMeaning: Two sorted integer arrays nums1 (length m) and nums2 (length n), where at least one array is non-empty.
understand.outputMeaning: A floating-point number: the middle element if m + n is odd, or the average of the two middle elements if m + n is even.
rules: Both input arrays are already sorted in non-decreasing order.
Total length N = m + n determines whether there is 1 center value (odd N) or 2 center values averaged together (even N).
Target optimal time complexity is O(log(min(m, n))).

terms.definition: The value(s) dividing a sorted dataset into equal lower and upper halves.
Choosing a cut point i in nums1 and j in nums2 so the left side holds half of all elements: i + j = Math.floor((m + n + 1) / 2).
Placeholder boundary values used when a cut sits at the very start (0 elements on left) or very end (0 elements on right) of an array.

example1.whyValid: Merged sorted order is [1, 2, 4, 8, 9] (length 5, odd). Cutting nums1 at i = 1 ([2] | [8]) and nums2 at j = 2 ([1, 4] | [9]) puts 3 elements on the left (1, 2, 4) and 2 on the right (8, 9). Max on left = max(2, 4) = 4, which is the median.

example2.whyEdgeCase: One array is completely empty and total length is even (2). The cut in nums1 is i = 0, so sentinels -Infinity/+Infinity prevent out-of-bounds reads, and the median averages (3 + 5) / 2 = 4.0.

dryRun.algorithmName: Binary Search Partition on Shorter Array

steps.title: Binary-search cut i in shorter array nums1 = [2, 8]
steps.description: Ensure nums1 is shorter (m=2, n=3). Half-size = (2 + 3 + 1) // 2 = 3. Search i in [0..2], starting at mid i = 1 -> j = 3 - 1 = 2.

state.caption: Check cross inequalities: A_left <= B_right and B_left <= A_right.

steps.title: Cross-check succeeds: 2 <= 9 and 4 <= 8
steps.description: Both inequalities hold! Because m + n = 5 is odd, the median is max(A_left, B_left) = max(2, 4) = 4.0.

state.caption: Valid partition found in 1 binary-search probe -> return 4.0.

approaches.name: Merge Both Sorted Arrays
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Merge nums1 and nums2 into a combined array, then pick the middle.
approaches.coreIdea: Use the standard two-pointer merge step from Merge Sort to create a single sorted array of length m + n, then read the median index(es).
steps: Allocate merged array of size m + n.
Merge nums1 and nums2 with two pointers.
If total is odd return merged[total / 2]; else return (merged[total/2 - 1] + merged[total/2]) / 2.0.
approaches.whyItWorks: Merging two sorted lists preserves sorted order across all elements.
approaches.whenToUse: Simple baseline when O(m + n) time and space are fine.

approaches.name: Two-Pointer Simulation (O(1) Space)
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Advance two pointers (m + n) / 2 steps tracking only the last two values.
approaches.coreIdea: Walk through the virtual merged sequence without storing it, retaining only prev and curr until reaching index (m + n) / 2.
steps: Set total = m + n and targetSteps = floor(total / 2) + 1.
Repeat targetSteps times: shift prev = curr, pick smaller head from nums1[i] or nums2[j] into curr.
Return curr if total is odd, else (prev + curr) / 2.0.
approaches.whyItWorks: Median only depends on the 1 or 2 values at the midpoint, so earlier merged values do not need to be retained.
approaches.whenToUse: When O(1) space is wanted and O(m + n) time is acceptable.

approaches.name: Binary Search Partition on Shorter Array
approaches.recommendedTradeOff: Achieves optimal O(log(min(m, n))) time and O(1) space by binary-searching the split index on the shorter array.
approaches.coreIdeaSummary: Binary-search cut i on the shorter array so left-half max <= right-half min.
approaches.coreIdea: Always binary-search on the shorter array A so j = half - i stays in bounds for B. Adjust i until A_left <= B_right and B_left <= A_right.
steps: If len(nums1) > len(nums2), swap them so nums1 has smaller length m.
Set half = floor((m + n + 1) / 2), lo = 0, hi = m.
Pick i = floor((lo + hi) / 2), j = half - i, and read boundary values using -Infinity/+Infinity sentinels.
If A_left <= B_right and B_left <= A_right, compute median from max(A_left, B_left) and min(A_right, B_right). Otherwise shift hi = i - 1 (when A_left > B_right) or lo = i + 1.
approaches.whyItWorks: Since both arrays are sorted, A_left <= A_right and B_left <= B_right already hold. Checking only the two cross inequalities ensures every element in the combined left half is <= every element in the combined right half.
approaches.whenToUse: Default optimal solution meeting the O(log(m + n)) constraint.
